segments.narration: Cartographers marked a massive landmass known as Sandy Island in the Coral Sea between Australia and New Caledonia, even though solid earth wasn't actually there.
The whaling ship Velocity reported the island in 1876. For more than a century, it was included on official maps around the world.
Mapmakers and digital services like National Geographic and Google Maps dutifully included the phantom territory for years. But nobody actually bothered to verify it in person.

That changed in 2012, when a team of Australian scientists sailed straight to the exact coordinates looking for geological anomalies. Instead of sandy beaches and palm trees, they found open ocean two miles deep.

The mystery was finally solved when geologists realized whalers in the nineteenth century had likely mischarted a massive floating raft of pumice stone thrown up by a sudden underwater volcano. How does an entire mountain of volcanic glass fool the British Navy for generations?

accuracy_flags.claim: Explorers dropped anchor on solid earth that didn't exist.
accuracy_flags.note: The reference states that the island was placed on maps by the whaling ship Velocity reporting breakers and 'Sandy Islets', and later kept through digital databases, but it does not state that explorers actually dropped anchor on it. Furthermore, 'dropped anchor on solid earth' is sensationalized since the island was a phantom.

accuracy_flags.claim: The British warship HMS Velocity officially charted Sandy Island in 1876.
accuracy_flags.note: The reference states the 'whaling ship Velocity' reported the fictitious island in 1876, not a British warship, and the source does not mention it being measured at 'nearly fifteen miles long'.

accuracy_flags.claim: National Geographic and Google Earth dutifully printed the phantom landmass for over a century.
accuracy_flags.note: Google Earth did not exist for 'over a century' (Google Maps/Earth were modern digital tools), and Google Earth's historical imagery actually showed a darkened sea. National Geographic and Google Maps included it until November 2012.

verdicts.claim: Whalers likely mischarted a massive floating raft of pumice stone thrown up by an underwater volcano.
verdicts.note: The reference explicitly discusses that the Velocity may have observed pumice sea rafts (masses of floating pumice ejected from an underwater volcano) traversing the area and mistakenly recorded them as an island.
